implementation_notes: Swift has no reader-writer lock in the standard library. The platform idiom is a concurrent DispatchQueue: reads are submitted normally and run concurrently, while writes are submitted with the .barrier flag, which makes the work item execute exclusively with respect to all other items on that queue - the queue is the lock and the barrier flag is the writer mode. This keeps readers from blocking each other, but it is asynchronous by nature: results must be obtained with queue.sync, and .barrier is meaningful only on a concurrent queue. Swift 6 concurrency adds actors (serialised, exclusive) and Synchronization.Mutex - neither is a reader-writer lock, so the queue idiom remains the idiomatic realization.
pitfalls: Barrier items are exclusive only on a concurrent queue; submitting .barrier to a serial queue silently behaves like an ordinary block.
queue.sync from inside the queue (or from a context that the queue is targeting) deadlocks - the classic DispatchQueue re-entrancy trap.
Dispatching expensive work to a concurrent queue consumes shared pool threads, and a blocking barrier item stalls every reader for its whole duration.
A read that returns a reference type still hands out shared mutable state; the barrier only orders the accesses that go through the queue.

variants.name: pthread_rwlock_t via the platform module
variants.implementation_notes: When a true blocking lock is required, Swift can drive the C primitive directly: pthread_rwlock_t is available through the platform module (Darwin on Apple platforms, Glibc on Linux), initialised once and destroyed in deinit. This is the only synchronous reader-writer lock on Apple platforms, so it suits APIs that cannot be expressed as queue dispatch; the priority policy is the OS's, and the same upgrade prohibition as everywhere else applies.
pitfalls: The rwlock must not be copied or used after deinit; keep it as a stable stored property and destroy it exactly once.
The POSIX priority policy is platform-defined; writer starvation is possible on read-preferring implementations.
Holding the lock across a throwing closure still releases it (defer), but calling back into the same lock from the body deadlocks - no re-entrancy.
